claim: The establishment and spread of antimalarial drug resistance vary drastically across different biogeographic regions.
source: The establishment and spread of antimalarial drug resistance vary drastically across different biogeographic regions.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the research question.

claim: Most malaria infections occur in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Though most infections occur in sub-Saharan Africa, resistant strains often emerge in low-transmission regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about malaria epidemiology.

claim: Resistant malaria strains often emerge in low-transmission regions.
source: Though most infections occur in sub-Saharan Africa, resistant strains often emerge in low-transmission regions.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: Existing models on resistance evolution lack consensus on the relationship between transmission intensity and drug resistance.
source: Existing models on resistance evolution lack consensus on the relationship between transmission intensity and drug resistance, possibly due to overlooking the feedback between antigenic diversity, host immunity, and selection for resistance.
evidence: This is supported by the review of previous models in the introduction.

claim: The model shows a negative correlation between parasite prevalence and resistance frequency, regardless of resistance cost or efficacy.
source: Our results show a negative correlation between parasite prevalence and resistance frequency, regardless of resistance cost or efficacy.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model simulations presented in the results.

claim: Chloroquine-resistant marker data supports the negative trend between prevalence and resistance frequency.
source: Validation using chloroquine-resistant marker data supports this trend.
evidence: This is supported by empirical data analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Post discontinuation of drugs, resistance remains high in low-diversity, low-transmission regions.
source: Post discontinuation of drugs, resistance remains high in low-diversity, low-transmission regions, while it steadily decreases in high-diversity, high-transmission regions.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: Post discontinuation of drugs, resistance steadily decreases in high-diversity, high-transmission regions.
source: Post discontinuation of drugs, resistance remains high in low-diversity, low-transmission regions, while it steadily decreases in high-diversity, high-transmission regions.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: Prolonged usage of antimicrobial drugs almost always results in the emergence and spread of resistant strains.
source: Prolonged usage of antimicrobial drugs almost always results in the emergence and spread of resistant strains (zur Wiesch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to zur Wiesch et al., 2011.

claim: The history of falciparum malaria chemotherapy over the last hundred years witnessed a succession of the spread of resistance to five classes of drugs region by region.
source: The history of falciparum malaria chemotherapy over the last hundred years witnessed a succession of the spread of resistance to five classes of drugs region by region (Blasco et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Blasco et al., 2017.

claim: Widespread resistant strains can almost always be traced back to Southeast Asia and South America.
source: Even though de novo-resistant alleles are constantly generated, widespread resistant strains can almost always be traced back to two unstable transmission regions, that is, Southeast Asia (especially the Greater Mekong Subregion) and South America (Ecker et al., 2012; Dondorp et al., 2009; Noedl et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ecker et al., 2012; Dondorp et al., 2009; Noedl et al., 2008.

claim: Frequencies of resistant genotypes often sweep close to fixation in Southeast Asia and South America under persistent drug usage.
source: While the frequencies of resistant genotypes often sweep close to fixation in these regions under persistent drug usage (Chaijaroenkul et al., 2011; Plummer et al., 2004), their frequencies are more variable in endemic transmission regions such as sub-Saharan Africa (Talisuna et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chaijaroenkul et al., 2011; Plummer et al., 2004.

claim: Resistant genotype frequencies are more variable in endemic transmission regions such as sub-Saharan Africa.
source: While the frequencies of resistant genotypes often sweep close to fixation in these regions under persistent drug usage (Chaijaroenkul et al., 2011; Plummer et al., 2004), their frequencies are more variable in endemic transmission regions such as sub-Saharan Africa (Talisuna et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Talisuna et al., 2002.

claim: In high-transmission regions, a steady decrease of resistant genotypes often ensues from reducing the particular drug usage.
source: More interestingly, while in high-transmission regions a steady decrease of resistant genotypes often ensues from reducing the particular drug usage (Narh et al., 2020; Hemming-Schroeder et al., 2018), resistant genotypes are maintained at high frequency in low or unstable transmission regions even after the abandonment of the drug for several decades (Lanteri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Narh et al., 2020; Hemming-Schroeder et al., 2018.

claim: Resistant genotypes are maintained at high frequency in low or unstable transmission regions even after the abandonment of the drug for several decades.
source: More interestingly, while in high-transmission regions a steady decrease of resistant genotypes often ensues from reducing the particular drug usage (Narh et al., 2020; Hemming-Schroeder et al., 2018), resistant genotypes are maintained at high frequency in low or unstable transmission regions even after the abandonment of the drug for several decades (Lanteri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lanteri et al., 2014.

claim: Orders of magnitude differentiate antigenic diversity of Plasmodium falciparum strains among biogeographic zones.
source: Yet, orders of magnitude differentiate antigenic diversity of Plasmodium falciparum strains among biogeographic zones and drive key differences in epidemiological features (Chen et al., 2011; Tonkin-Hill et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2011; Tonkin-Hill et al., 2018.

claim: Hyper-diverse antigens of parasites in sub-Saharan Africa emerged from the long-term co-evolutionary arms race among hosts, vectors, and parasites.
source: Hyper-diverse antigens of parasites in sub-Saharan Africa emerged from the long-term co-evolutionary arms race among hosts, vectors, and parasites (Volkman et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Volkman et al., 2001.

claim: Hosts in endemic regions of falciparum malaria do not develop sterile immunity and can constantly get reinfected with reduced symptoms.
source: In endemic regions of falciparum malaria, hosts do not develop sterile immunity and can constantly get reinfected with reduced symptoms (Day and Marsh, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Day and Marsh, 1991.

claim: Asymptomatic carriers of the parasite still constitute part of the transmission and serve as a reservoir of strain diversity.
source: These asymptomatic carriers of the parasite still constitute part of the transmission and serve as a reservoir of strain diversity (Tiedje et al., 2017; Bonnet et al., 2003) despite the fact that parasite prevalence decreases with host age in endemic regions (Aron, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tiedje et al., 2017; Bonnet et al., 2003.

claim: Parasite prevalence decreases with host age in endemic regions.
source: These asymptomatic carriers of the parasite still constitute part of the transmission and serve as a reservoir of strain diversity (Tiedje et al., 2017; Bonnet et al., 2003) despite the fact that parasite prevalence decreases with host age in endemic regions (Aron, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Aron, 1983.

claim: P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1) is encoded by var genes, a gene family of 60 different copies within a single parasite genome.
source: One of the major surface proteins, P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1), is encoded by var genes, a gene family of 60 different copies within a single parasite genome (Rask et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rask et al., 2010.

claim: Immune selection maintains the composition of var genes between different strains with minimal overlap.
source: Immune selection maintains the composition of var genes between different strains with minimal overlap (He et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to He et al., 2018.

claim: Whether the hosts have seen the specific variants of the var genes largely determines the clearance rate of the parasites.
source: Whether the hosts have seen the specific variants of the var genes largely determines the clearance rate of the parasites (Barry et al., 2011; Djimdé et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barry et al., 2011; Djimdé et al., 2003.

claim: The range of transmission potential that leads to the highest prevalence given a specific strain diversity increases from low diversity to high diversity.
source: We observe that the range of transmission potential that leads to the highest prevalence given a specific strain diversity increases from low diversity to high diversity (see gray area in Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The prevalence decreases under drug treatment, but maintains the same relationship with strain diversity and transmission potential as that without treatment.
source: The prevalence decreases under drug treatment, but maintains the same relationship with strain diversity and transmission potential as that without treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Strain diversity in Africa is much higher than in other continents.
source: As expected, strain diversity in Africa is much higher than in other continents, while transmission potential varies widely within continents, with overlaps in medium ranges.
evidence: This is based on empirical data compiled from literature and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Transmission potential varies widely within continents, with overlaps in medium ranges.
source: As expected, strain diversity in Africa is much higher than in other continents, while transmission potential varies widely within continents, with overlaps in medium ranges.
evidence: This is based on empirical data compiled from literature and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Strain diversity in Africa and Asia tracks the range of transmission potential.
source: Interestingly, while strain diversity in Africa and Asia tracks the range of transmission potential, Oceania and South America have lower strain diversity than expected by transmission potential.
evidence: This is an observation from the empirical data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Oceania and South America have lower strain diversity than expected by transmission potential.
source: Interestingly, while strain diversity in Africa and Asia tracks the range of transmission potential, Oceania and South America have lower strain diversity than expected by transmission potential.
evidence: This is an observation from the empirical data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The frequency of resistance decreases with increasing parasite prevalence.
source: In general, the frequency of resistance decreases with increasing parasite prevalence (Figure 2B and C), except for very low transmission potential, where resistance always fixes because wild-type strains cannot sustain transmissions under treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: At very low transmission potential, resistance always fixes because wild-type strains cannot sustain transmissions under treatment.
source: In general, the frequency of resistance decreases with increasing parasite prevalence (Figure 2B and C), except for very low transmission potential, where resistance always fixes because wild-type strains cannot sustain transmissions under treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with explanation.

claim: The fitness costs of single- and mixed-genotype infections, symptomatic treatment rate, and the efficacy of drug resistance only influence the slope of the relationship between prevalence and resistance frequency and the range of coexistence of resistant and wild-type parasites, but do not alter the negative relationship qualitatively.
source: The fitness costs of single- and mixed-genotype infections, symptomatic treatment rate, and the efficacy of drug resistance only influence the slope of the relationship and the range of coexistence of resistant and wild-type parasites, but do not alter the negative relationship qualitatively (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 2C and supplements.

claim: The negative relationship between resistance and prevalence holds even when resistant genotypes have zero cost in transmissibility.
source: Note that the negative relationship holds even when resistant genotypes have zero cost in transmissibility: they might still coexist instead of fix under very high disease prevalence (green dots in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Samples from Asia and South America cluster around low-prevalence and high-resistance regions.
source: Samples from Asia and South America cluster around low-prevalence and high-resistance regions, with Asian samples having more variation in resistance, whilst samples from Oceania and Africa display a wide range of prevalence and resistance frequency.
evidence: This is an observation from the empirical data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Samples from Oceania and Africa display a wide range of prevalence and resistance frequency.
source: Samples from Asia and South America cluster around low-prevalence and high-resistance regions, with Asian samples having more variation in resistance, whilst samples from Oceania and Africa display a wide range of prevalence and resistance frequency.
evidence: This is an observation from the empirical data shown in Figure 4.

claim: When drug treatments are applied in a wild-type-only transmission setting, parasite prevalence is significantly reduced.
source: When drug treatments are applied in a wild-type-only transmission setting, parasite prevalence is significantly reduced (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as is host generalized immunity (Figure 5A, upper panel).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5A.

claim: The proportion of hosts in drug-treated status increases under higher diversity.
source: In addition, the proportion of hosts in drug-treated status increases under higher diversity.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: If the resistant genotype is present in the parasite population and starts invading when the drug is applied, hosts' generalized immunity is comparable at equilibrium to that of the no-treatment scenario.
source: If instead the resistant genotype is present in the parasite population and starts invading when the drug is applied, hosts' generalized immunity is comparable at equilibrium to that of the no-treatment scenario (Figure 5, lower panel).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Resistance invasion boosts host immunity to a similar level before drug treatment.
source: In the meantime, resistance invasion boosts host immunity to a similar level before drug treatment (Figure 6, upper panel).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: Under a low-diversity scenario, wild-type parasites quickly go extinct.
source: Under a low-diversity scenario, wild-type parasites quickly go extinct (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Low-diversity scenarios suffer the slowest decline in resistant genotypes after switching to different drugs.
source: In our model, low-diversity scenarios suffer the slowest decline in resistant genotypes after switching to different drugs.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: Resistance frequency plunges quickly in high-diversity regions when the drug policy changes.
source: In contrast, resistance frequency plunges quickly in high-diversity regions when the drug policy changes (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: Resistant genotypes have a much higher fitness advantage in low-diversity regions even with reduced drug usage because infected hosts are still highly symptomatic.
source: Two processes are responsible for the observed trend. First, resistant genotypes have a much higher fitness advantage in low-diversity regions even with reduced drug usage because infected hosts are still highly symptomatic; this trend holds even if diversity is decoupled with transmission potential: given the same transmission potential, high-diversity scenarios have a faster percentage of reduction in resistance (see Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an explanation of the model findings with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: If low transmission potential is coupled with low diversity, the rate of change in parasite populations is slower due to longer generation intervals between transmission events.
source: Second, if low transmission potential is coupled with low diversity, the rate of change in parasite populations is slower due to longer generation intervals between transmission events.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model findings.

claim: The transition of the first-line drug to ACT in Africa, such as Ghana and Kenya, resulted in a fast reduction in resistant genotypes.
source: This pattern corroborates similar observations across different biogeographic areas: while the transition of the first-line drug to ACT in Africa, such as Ghana and Kenya, resulted in a fast reduction in resistant genotypes, the reduction was only minor in Oceania, and resistant genotypes are still maintained at almost fixation in Southeast Asia and South America despite the change in the first-line drugs occurring more than 30 y ago (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on empirical data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The reduction in resistant genotypes was only minor in Oceania after drug policy change.
source: This pattern corroborates similar observations across different biogeographic areas: while the transition of the first-line drug to ACT in Africa, such as Ghana and Kenya, resulted in a fast reduction in resistant genotypes, the reduction was only minor in Oceania, and resistant genotypes are still maintained at almost fixation in Southeast Asia and South America despite the change in the first-line drugs occurring more than 30 y ago (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on empirical data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Resistant genotypes are still maintained at almost fixation in Southeast Asia and South America despite the change in the first-line drugs occurring more than 30 years ago.
source: This pattern corroborates similar observations across different biogeographic areas: while the transition of the first-line drug to ACT in Africa, such as Ghana and Kenya, resulted in a fast reduction in resistant genotypes, the reduction was only minor in Oceania, and resistant genotypes are still maintained at almost fixation in Southeast Asia and South America despite the change in the first-line drugs occurring more than 30 y ago (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on empirical data shown in Figure 8.

claim: A generalized-immunity-only model produces a valley phenomenon where resistance frequency is both high at the two ends of prevalence.
source: We observe a valley phenomenon (i.e., resistance frequency is both high at the two ends of prevalence; Figure 9), which is qualitatively similar to Artzy-Randrup et al., 2010.
evidence: This is a finding from the generalized-immunity-only model shown in Figure 9.

claim: In the generalized-immunity-only model, following the switch of first-line drugs, the medium-transmission region has the fastest reduction in resistance frequency, followed by the high- and low-transmission regions.
source: Similarly, following the switch of first-line drugs, the medium-transmission region has the fastest reduction in resistance frequency, followed by the high- and low-transmission regions.
evidence: This is a finding from the generalized-immunity-only model.

claim: The comparison between the full model versus the generalized-immunity-only model emphasizes the importance of incorporating antigenic diversity to generate a negative relationship between resistance and prevalence.
source: The comparison between the full model versus the generalized-immunity-only model emphasizes the importance of incorporating antigenic diversity to generate a negative relationship between resistance and prevalence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the two models.

claim: Past models failed to reproduce the observed patterns of monotonic decreasing trend of resistance frequency with prevalence despite varying resistance costs, access to treatments, or resistance efficacy.
source: While past models have examined the frequency of drug resistance as a consequence of transmission intensity and generalized immunity, these models, unlike ours, failed to reproduce the observed patterns of monotonic decreasing trend of resistance frequency with prevalence despite varying resistance costs, access to treatments, or resistance efficacy.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous models.

claim: The model formulation directly links selection pressure from drug usage with local transmission dynamics through the interaction between strain-specific immunity, generalized immunity, and host immune response.
source: This contrast stems from two main innovations of our model. First, its formulation directly links selection pressure from drug usage with local transmission dynamics through the interaction between strain-specific immunity, generalized immunity, and host immune response.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model.

claim: The model relies on a macroparasitic modeling structure suitable for diseases with high variation in cooccurring infections and strain diversities.
source: Second, this formulation relies on a macroparasitic modeling structure suitable for diseases with high variation in cooccurring infections and strain diversities (Anderson and May, 1978).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model with citation.

claim: When a fixed fraction of hosts is assumed to be drug-treated upon infection, the frequency of resistance is found to be unrelated to transmission intensity or requires other mechanisms to explain why resistance is prevalent in low-transmission regions.
source: For example, when a fixed fraction of hosts is assumed to be drug-treated upon infection (e.g., in Curtis and Otoo, 1986; Dye and Williams, 1997; Hastings, 1997; Koella and Antia, 2003), the frequency of resistance is found to be unrelated to transmission intensity or requires other mechanisms to explain why resistance is prevalent in low-transmission regions.
evidence: This is a critique of previous models with citations.

claim: Replication rates of resistant parasites are consistently found to be slower such that they produce less parasitemia during the infection than wild-type parasites.
source: On the one hand, replication rates of resistant parasites are consistently found to be slower such that they produce less parasitemia during the infection than wild-type parasites (Bushman et al., 2016; Koella, 1893; de Roode et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bushman et al., 2016; Koella, 1893; de Roode et al., 2005.

claim: Field studies show that the transmissibility of resistant parasites could be partially compensated by a higher gametocyte production.
source: On the other hand, field studies also show that the transmissibility could be partially compensated by a higher gametocyte production (reviewed in Koella, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koella, 1998.

claim: Within-host competition between resistant and wild-type infections results in a higher cost for resistant infections than in single-genotype infections.
source: Empirical and modeling studies Bushman et al., 2016; Bushman et al., 2018; de Roode et al., 2004 have shown that within-host competition between resistant and wild-type infections results in a higher cost for resistant infections than in single-genotype infections.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bushman et al., 2016; Bushman et al., 2018; de Roode et al., 2004.

claim: The model assumes that a single locus determines resistance.
source: First, it currently assumes that a single locus determines resistance.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the model.

claim: Rates of recombination could strongly influence the spread and maintenance of resistance when resistance is encoded or augmented by two or more loci.
source: If resistance is encoded or augmented by two or more loci (e.g., ACT or SP), past population genetic models demonstrate that rates of recombination could strongly influence the spread and maintenance of resistance (Dye and Williams, 1997; Hastings, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dye and Williams, 1997; Hastings, 2006.

claim: Preexisting partner-drug-resistant genotypes promote the establishment of Artemisinin resistance.
source: Recent models have shown that preexisting partner-drug-resistant genotypes promote the establishment of Artemisinin resistance (Watson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Watson et al., 2022.

claim: A high selfing rate in low transmission ensures high linkage among multilocus resistance, promoting their higher frequencies.
source: These earlier population genetics models of drug resistance posit that a high selfing rate in low transmission ensures high linkage among multilocus resistance, promoting their higher frequencies (Dye and Williams, 1997; Hastings and D'Alessandro, 2000; Hastings and Donnelly, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dye and Williams, 1997; Hastings and D'Alessandro, 2000; Hastings and Donnelly, 2005.

claim: The deterministic compartmental model does not consider genetic drift.
source: Second, our deterministic compartmental model does not consider several sources of variation in parasite transmission. Genetic drift is not incorporated in the model, which could influence the variation of strain frequencies at the population level due to severe bottlenecks during vector transmission (Wong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the model with citation.

claim: Empirical evidence of parasite burdens is usually over-dispersed in that relatively few members of the host population harbor the majority of the parasite population.
source: Empirical evidence of parasite burdens is usually over-dispersed in that relatively few members of the host population harbor the majority of the parasite population (Anderson and Gordon, 1982; Churcher et al., 2005; Grogan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anderson and Gordon, 1982; Churcher et al., 2005; Grogan et al., 2016.

claim: The model assumed a random association between resistant genotype and antigenic diversity.
source: Lastly, our model assumed a random association between resistant genotype and antigenic diversity.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model.

claim: In the early stage of invasion, the resistant genotype should have a limited antigenic background until it becomes widespread.
source: In reality, in the early stage of invasion, the resistant genotype should have a limited antigenic background until it becomes widespread.
evidence: This is a discussion of model limitations.

claim: Selection for high antigenic variation in high transmission slows the spread of resistance.
source: In an agent-based stochastic model, Whitlock et al., 2021 found that selection for high antigenic variation in high transmission slows the spread of resistance.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Whitlock et al., 2021.

claim: The model predicts an equilibrium state of resistance frequency under persistent drug usage, which cannot be extrapolated to transient dynamics of new drug introduction.
source: It is also to be noted that the trend found in our model predicts an equilibrium state of resistance frequency under persistent drug usage, which cannot be extrapolated to transient dynamics of new drug introduction.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the model.

claim: The Pfcrt 76T mutation is essential for chloroquine resistance.
source: Therefore, we focused on empirical comparison to Pfcrt 76T because this mutation is essential for chloroquine resistance (Ecker et al., 2012) and chloroquine has been heavily used as first-line drugs for years in most countries.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ecker et al., 2012.

claim: Control protocols should vary from region to region and there is no one-size-fits-all cure for malaria control worldwide.
source: In sum, we show that strain diversity and associated strain-specific host immunity, dynamically tracked through the macroparasitic structure, can predict the complex relationship between transmission intensity and drug resistance frequencies. Our model implies that control protocols should vary from region to region and that there is no one-size-fits-all cure for malaria control worldwide (Rasmussen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model with citation.

claim: In regions of low prevalence, such as Southeast Asia, long-term goals for malaria prevention will likely not be aided by intensive drug treatment.
source: In regions of low prevalence, such as Southeast Asia, long-term goals for malaria prevention will likely not be aided by intensive drug treatment (Delacollette et al., 2009; Imwong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model with citations.

claim: In low-prevalence regions, elimination of falciparum malaria through vector control measures could proceed with little effect on drug resistance levels.
source: In these regions, elimination of falciparum malaria through vector control measures could proceed with little effect on drug resistance levels, whereas continual drug treatment will almost certainly cause fixation or near-fixation of resistance for a prolonged period of time, even after discontinuation of one drug.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model.

claim: In high-prevalence regions such as sub-Saharan Africa, measures of prompt switching between first-line drugs and combination therapies will be quite robust against rapid increases and prolonged maintenance of drug resistance.
source: In contrast, in high-prevalence regions such as sub-Saharan Africa, measures of prompt switching between first-line drugs and combination therapies will be quite robust against rapid increases and prolonged maintenance of drug resistance (Flegg et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model with citation.

claim: The infectivity of falciparum malaria patients to mosquitoes was estimated to be around 0.1 from multiple studies.
source: The infectivity of falciparum malaria patients to mosquitoes was estimated to be around 0.1 from multiple studies (Timinao et al., 2021; Coleman et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Timinao et al., 2021; Coleman et al., 2004.

claim: Transmissibility from infected mosquitoes to naïve hosts is around 0.8 for sporozoites density higher than 1000 per mosquito.
source: Transmissibility from infected mosquitoes to naïve hosts is around 0.8 for sporozoites density higher than 1000 per mosquito (Churcher et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Churcher et al., 2005.

claim: Parasites are assumed to be distributed independently and randomly among hosts within the same compartment.
source: Since hosts can harbor multiple parasite strains, parasites are assumed to be distributed independently and randomly among hosts within the same compartment (Anderson and May, 1978).
evidence: This is a model assumption with citation.

claim: The number of unique strains ranges from 6 to 447, which corresponds to a pool of 360 to 27,000 unique surface antigens.
source: Specifically, the number of unique strains ranges from 6 to 447, which corresponds to a pool of 360 (typical of low-transmission regions) to 27,000 unique surface antigens (typical of sub-Saharan Africa) (Chen et al., 2011; Tonkin-Hill et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the parameter range used in the model with citations.

claim: The model follows the pattern of transmissions through mosquito bites using a sinusoidal curve, representing a peak transmission period in the wet season, and low transmission in the dry season annually.
source: We model the pattern of transmissions through mosquito bites following a sinusoidal curve (Appendix 1), representing a peak transmission period in the wet season, and low transmission in the dry season annually, with a mean transmission potential from 0.007 to 5.8.
evidence: This describes the model structure.
